title: Brythons
capsule: As a people, the Brythons (Common Brittonic-speaking Celtic Britons) inhabited most of Great Britain south of the Forth-Clyde line through the Roman period and after Roman withdrawal in the early 5th century, when Anglo-Saxon, Irish, and Pictish pressure fragmented their territory into numerous separate kingdoms. Brythonic-speaking communities also migrated overseas in this period, founding Brittany in Armorica and the short-lived Britonia in northwestern Spain. Over the following centuries Brythonic political and linguistic identity narrowed mainly to Wales, Cornwall/Dumnonia, and Cumbric-speaking Strathclyde (annexed by Scotland in the 11th century), with independent Welsh rule persisting into the 13th century.
attestation: Boundaries from Seshat Cliopatria (Bennett et al., Scientific Data 2025; CC BY 4.0), digitized from standard historical atlases at ~0.07° resolution. The Brythons are not a single bounded polity; the dataset geometry likely represents their collective presence across Britain as reconstructed from archaeological and linguistic evidence. Pre-Roman extents are broadly estimated; Roman-period territories are better documented, and post-Roman Brythonic kingdoms are reconstructed from early medieval Welsh chronicles and genealogical texts with significant uncertainty about boundaries.
